
## Analysis using Neural Networks


As a second predictive approach we forecast taxi demand with feed-forward neural networks (NNs). Demand is not a simple additive function of a given set of features: spatial, temporal, and local context (points of interest, weather) interact non-linearly with each other. A linear model such as our ridge benchmark captures only some of this and shifts the burden onto manual feature engineering, whereas a network discovers the relevant combinations directly during training. We judge the networks against two benchmarks: a ridge regression and a historical-mean predictor (mean `trip_count` per cell $\times$ hour-of-day in the training period). The latter is a demanding baseline, and whether the added flexibility of a network actually beats this cheap lookup is what this chapter sets out to establish.

### Evaluation method

Our client wants to understand ride-hailing demand dynamics in Chicago, so we aim to provide a clear image about the power of NN predictions for the client to answer operational questions a fleet operator would ask: can simple NNs predict demand reliably, and is the gain over the near-free historical mean large enough to justify building, tuning and retraining them? Which data serves demand prediction best (H3 hexagons vs. community areas, hourly or coarser buckets)?

We evaluate our models along two dimensions: first by comparing the three architectures within a fixed resolution, where MAE and $R^2$ together give a precise, intuitive image on performance, and second by comparing across temporal (1 h, 2 h, 6 h, 24 h) and spatial resolutions (community areas vs. H3 hexagons), where we lean on MAPE and $R^2$ for scale-independence while keeping MAE as a tangible reference for non-technical readers.

Behind these headline figures we record RMSE, NRMSE (raw and log scale) and a zero-demand accuracy score for empty cells, and we plot per-epoch learning curves to diagnose overfitting. To gauge whether a network's error distribution differs from a benchmark's beyond chance, we run a Wilcoxon signed-rank test against each. It is worth stating plainly what this test can and cannot do: it indicates whether two error distributions differ on this particular sample, not whether the operator should deploy a network. That decision is a cost–benefit one, taken up in the conclusion. The significance test only orients us toward configurations worth costing out.

### Architecture and training

We compare three fully connected architectures that differ only in capacity — a **baseline** (2 hidden layers $\times$ 64 units), a **deeper** model (8 $\times$ 64) and a **wider** model (2 $\times$ 256) — each evaluated across the four time buckets and two spatial units. After sweeping optimizers, activations and losses, we settled on the configuration that gave the best performance for the least added complexity: ReLU activations with He/Kaiming-normal initialization (which balances weight variances across layers and reduces the chance of unstable starts), and stochastic gradient descent with momentum. A cell's spatial identity (a community area or H3 hexagon) is fed as a jointly learned 16-dimensional embedding concatenated with the standardized numeric features, so that similar locations sit near one another in a learned space.

The most consequential choice is the training objective, because demand is over-dispersed, zero-inflated count data. MSE would assume symmetric constant-variance errors and allow negative predictions; a Poisson likelihood respects the counts but assumes variance equals mean, which ours violates. For the 1 h, 2 h and 6 h models we therefore minimize the **negative binomial (NB2) negative log-likelihood**, which models the variance explicitly and does not assume balanced mean and variance. The network (with NB2 training loss) returns a prediction in log space that is exponentiated back to the original demand scale. Because $\exp(\cdot)$ grows steeply, a small log-space error becomes a large count error, and at daily aggregation (where demand averages ~180 (CA) to ~420 (hex) per day) a minor overshoot can explode into millions of predicted trips and destabilize training. The 24 h models are consequently trained on **MAE over the log1p scale** instead; their loss values and learning curves are therefore not directly comparable to the finer horizons, and only the raw-count evaluation metrics below can be compared across all buckets.

Learning rate and weight decay are tuned per architecture by a two-stage grid search. First, a sweep over `2e-5`–`8e-2` locates the right decade, then a fine sweep within it. Each candidate is evaluated with a short patience of 5 (to save computation time) and a single seed to keep the search affordable, before the winner is retrained under the full schedule. Overfitting is held in check by that decoupled weight decay and by early stopping on validation loss (patience 10, best-weight restoration). The data are split 70/15/15 into train/validation/test sets. The split is positional (`shuffle=False`), so validation and test are the tail of the dataframe rather than a random draw despite the `SPLIT="random"` label in the code.

### Expectations

We formulated five hypotheses before training.

1. The NNs should clearly beat the linear ridge, since demand responds non-linearly to hour, location and weather.
2. They should at least match the historical mean by learning the cell $\times$ hour interaction, and surpass it by using information the lookup cannot — weekday, holidays, weather deviations.
3. More capacity should help modestly, with the deep variant most exposed to optimization instability.
4. The NN advantage should be largest at fine temporal granularity, where samples are plentiful and day-to-day fluctuation matters, and shrink or vanish at daily buckets, where data volume collapses and the stable mean pattern dominates.
5. Hyperparameters — the learning rate above all — should matter more than architecture.

Four findings stand out. **Tuning dominates architecture** (hypothesis 5): untuned, every architecture lands far below its tuned counterpart, and the deep model occasionally produces strongly negative $R^2$ from a handful of exploded predictions — most visibly at Hex-6 6h, where the untuned wide model collapses to $R^2 = -0.267$ — while its deviance-based $D^2$ stays around 0.85, showing these are tail artefacts of the exponential link, not globally broken models. **The granularity pattern matches hypothesis 4**: the tuned networks beat the historical mean cleanly at 1–2 h on every metric, roughly tie at 6 h (better MAE and MAPE, but worse RMSE and $R^2$ — the mean wins $R^2$ 0.846 vs 0.815 at CA-6h and 0.858 vs 0.826 at Hex-6h), and at 24 h the tuned network still leads on MAE and $R^2$ but the gap narrows as the averaging horizon smooths the target. **Capacity helps only after tuning**: the tuned deep model is strongest at fine granularity (best at CA and Hex 1h and 2h), while the tuned baseline takes over at the coarsest buckets (6h and 24h); untuned, the deep and wide models are the most fragile. Finally, two ablations tracked the earlier feature analysis — removing the weather block at 2 h did not hurt (weather had near-zero permutation importance), and sigmoid matched ReLU at 1 h.

### Exemplary walkthrough (H3 resolution 6, hourly)

The hourly hexagon configuration illustrates the pipeline. It covers 33 hexagons over 289k cell-hours; 35.8 % of test rows are zero-demand and mean test demand is 17.6 trips. Ridge reaches $R^2 = 0.59$ — beaten by every tuned network (hypothesis 1) — while the historical mean sets the real bar at $R^2 = 0.833$, MAE $= 7.24$. An untuned baseline (lr $5 \cdot 10^{-5}$) reaches only $R^2 \approx 0.78$, undertrained; grid search moves it to lr 0.04, weight decay $5 \cdot 10^{-3}$ and $R^2 = 0.844$, above the benchmark. The tuned deep model (lr $6 \cdot 10^{-3}$, weight decay $3 \cdot 10^{-3}$) reaches **$R^2 = 0.859$, MAE $= 6.36$** — $\approx 12\%$ lower mean error than the benchmark, achieved precisely where the lookup is blind: day-to-day deviations from the average hex-hour pattern.

### Conclusion and interpretation for the business case

The tuned networks beat the plain historical-average lookup on MAE at **every** resolution, so the Neural Networks do add value to the predictions. That alone, however, does not mean the client should implement them. Whether the gain is *worth implementing* is a cost question the significance tests cannot answer, and it turns on how large and how stable that edge actually is.

The size of the edge over the historical mean is **unstable across temporal resolutions**. The MAE reduction is roughly 13–15 % at the 1 h and 2 h resolutions, shrinks to only ~3 % at 6 h, and widens again to ~21–24 % at 24 h. At the 6 h level, in particular, there is essentially no meaningful difference between the historical mean and the networks — the mean even reclaims RMSE and $R^2$ there, leaving the network a MAE-only advantage at zero marginal cost. For repositioning idle taxis, planning shifts and anticipating local surges, the actionable resolution is the hourly-to-two-hourly hexagon forecast, and it is precisely there that the networks earn their keep: MAE around 6.36 vs. 7.24 at 1 h and 12.05 vs. 13.88 at 2 h (against a mean of ~17.6 trips), with the NB model's strictly positive outputs directly readable as expected pickups.

Which architecture wins also depends on data density. At the more granular resolutions (1 h, 2 h) the more complex models, especially the tuned deeper model outperforms the simpler baseline, but at the sparse, coarse resolutions the simpler baseline takes over. This is a **data-sparsity effect**: with few samples the true non-linear structure is under-determined, so a high-capacity model fits sampling variance instead of signal — precisely overfitting, with the variance term of its error dominating. With more data the non-linear structure sharpens and is better identified by the higher-capacity models. The upshot is that **there is no single best model across both dimensions**, and different temporal resolutions may serve different purposes: 1 h/2 h forecasts are better suited to (real-time) fleet rebalancing, while 6 h/24 h forecasts may be more useful for financial planning of profits and costs, so the model should be chosen based on the use case rather than the resolution based on the model performance.

Weighing cost against benefit makes the recommendation concrete. The benefit is real but bounded and uneven across temporal resolutions, the costs are not. A network requires a per-configuration two-stage learning-rate and weight-decay search to build, an exponential link fragile enough that an untuned model can be *worse* than the free benchmark, demanding careful re-tuning whenever the data shift, recurring retraining, divergence monitoring and serving infrastructure to operate, and a loss of the full transparency the lookup offers.

The historical mean, by contrast, costs essentially nothing, needs no tuning and stays interpretable. The network therefore only justifies itself where its sharper predictions deliver enough operational value to justify the ongoing cost of running it.

::: {.callout-note title="Caveats and open items"}
Several caveats and open items bound this reading. Most runs use a single seed, so small $R^2$ gaps should not be over-read; the daily models optimize a different loss (log1p-MAE) on a different scale, so their training curves are not comparable to the NB2 horizons; and the NB2 likelihood addresses over-dispersion in the mean only, not exact zero-demand probabilities. We also did not benchmark training or inference speed or scalability, which leaves real-time retraining viability unsettled, and we did not convert accuracy into money — the decisive input for the cost–benefit above.
:::

Nonetheless the networks hold clear potential and warrant further testing: on larger-scale data, with other architectures, and with alternative training strategies — notably, we aggregated trips into counts *before* training, and learning from the disaggregated trip level (e.g. via spatio-temporal point-process models) is a promising direction worth evaluating. For deployment we recommend a pragmatic hybrid: the historical hex-hour mean as an always-available, near-free fallback — or, in future work, an input feature — with the tuned NB network supplying the fine-grained hourly corrections wherever the repositioning value justifies its upkeep.
